t: Count Pairs Whose Sum is Less than Target
o: Count index pairs i < j with nums[i]+nums[j] < target. With n ≤ 50, an O(n²) double loop is perfectly fine. The classic optimization is sorting plus two pointers: after sorting, for each left index i, count how many j > i satisfy the condition using a shrinking right pointer, achieving O(n log n). Example 1: sorted [-1,1,1,2,3], target 2 → pairs (−1,1),(−1,1),(−1,2)… careful counting yields 3 valid original-index pairs; the two-pointer method counts value pairs correctly since order within a pair doesn't matter.
k: Sorting doesn't affect the pair count since i<j ordering is irrelevant to the sum condition.
Two pointers: fix left, move right pointer leftward while the sum is too large; then all indices between contribute.

a.i: Directly test all n(n−1)/2 pairs — trivially fits constraints.

Sort ascending. Fix left pointer l; start right pointer r at n−1. While nums[l]+nums[r] ≥ target, decrement r. Then every index in (l, r] paired with l works, adding r−l pairs; advance l. Total O(n log n).
s: l = 0, r = n−1; while l < r: if nums[l]+nums[r] < target, add r−l and l++; else r−−.

w: Brute force suffices here; show two pointers to demonstrate the scalable pattern (needed when n is large). Pitfall: strict inequality (<, not ≤), and in JavaScript remember the default sort is lexicographic. Follow-up: count pairs with sum ≤ target, or k-sum variants.
